#### First stratum: endemic radiations (Late Cretaceous--middle Eocene) {.unnumbered}

Simpson's first stratum characterises the early phase of South American mammal evolution in the aftermath of the continent's isolation (@fig-SALMA). It is thought to have lasted from the Late Cretaceous/early Palaeocene to the late middle Eocene. Mammal at that time are often referred to as the continent's 'original inhabitants'. These would include endemic metatherians (@fig-persistence A), native ungulates (@fig-persistence C), xenarthrans (@fig-persistence B), as well as a few remnant non-therian lineages (*e*.*g*., Gondwanatheria).

The oldest Cenozoic South American land mammalian assemblages date back to the early Palaeocene. These have been recovered from the Punta Peligro (Argentina) and Tiupampa (Bolivia) localities (@fig-MapLoc), each leading to the recognition of the oldest intervals of the South American Land Mammal Age (SALMA) scale, namely, the Peligran and the Tiupampan (@fig-SALMA). Biochronological evidence suggests the Tiupampan SALMA to be older than the Peligran SALMA, and corroborate an age interval of 64.5--64 Ma for the Tiupampan fauna [@gelfo2009]. An additional occurrence of pre-Tiumpampan therian mammal was recovered from the Grenier Farm locality (@fig-MapLoc), and was assigned to the extinct metatherian order Polydolopimorphia [@goin2006; @fig-persistence A].

The faunal composition of the Tiupampan and Peligran assemblages delivered precious insights into the early Cenozoic history of South American mammals. The great metatherian diversity (@fig-persistence A), together with the presence of representatives from several ungulate-related lineages typically found in the Northern hemisphere (formerly grouped into the 'condylarths'), suggested that South American mammalian assemblages received significant faunal supply from North America between the Late Cretaceous and the early Palaeocene [@pascual2006]. Geological evidence corroborated the possibility for intermediate episodic connections between the two continents in that interval [@pascual2006], possibly also involving the Caribbean islands [@viñola-lópez2022]. As an echo to the name 'Great American Biotic Interchange' (see @sec-SAFauna and @sec-chap3), this keystone biotic exchange for the architecture of Simpson's first stratum was thus termed 'First American Biotic Interchange' (FABI) [@goin_origin_2012].

Along with these therian lineages of North American affinity, non-therian lineages persisted in South America at least until the mid-Palaeogene, thus well after the Cretaceous--Palaeogene boundary [@goin_gondwana_2012]. The most fascinating example of non-therian lineage persistence known to date is probably the enigmatic *Necrolestes*, from the Santa Cruz Formation (early Miocene, Santacrucian SALMA, see @fig-SALMA), identified as a remnant of the clade Meridiolestida, a mammal group that thrived from the Late Jurassic up until the Late Cretaceous [@rougier2012; @chimento2012].

Younger assemblages characteristic of Simpson's first stratum notably include the São José de Itaboraí (often abbreviated Itaboraí) fauna (@fig-MapLoc), one of the most diverse in the Palaeogene of South Ameri*ca*. It led to the Itaboraian SALMA, approximately dating back to 53 Ma (@fig-SALMA). The Itaboraian fauna is still dominated by metatherians [@goin2016]. It also revealed that all the higher South American Native Ungulate (SANU) lineages were clearly differentiated at that time (@fig-persistence C). More importantly, the Itaboraian fauna yielded the oldest known occurrence of armadillo (Xenarthra: Cingulata) [@bergqvist2004], thus documenting the appearance of Xenarthra in the fossil record (@fig-persistence B). The late appearance of xenarthrans in the fossil record remains an enigma for South American mammal palaeontology, and has been referred to as the 'xenarthran mystery' [@goin2016]. Indeed, as suggested by their name meaning "weird articulations", xenarthrans, today represented by sloths, anteaters and armadillos, share very derived morphological characters that are not found in any other known eutherian mammal lineage. Molecular evidence suggests that they form a clade with the african group Afrotheria, called 'Atlantogenata', literally meaning "generated by the Atlantic ocean", and thus, would have diverged from their sister-group following the break-up of Gondwana, some 120 Ma [@waddell1999]. Why armadillos only appear in the fossil record *ca*. 53 Ma, and sloths in the Late Oligocene (see next section), whereas their divergence with other South American eutherians largely predates the earliest known mammal assemblages found on the continent thus remains an open question.

Younger assemblages of the first stratum progressively record a turnover in the relative proportion of metatherian vs. eutherian mammals in the communities, with an increasing dominance of eutherians, that several authors related to the gradual Eocene climate cooling from *ca*. 50 Ma onwards [@goin2016; @croft_horned_2016; @westerhold2020]. Later in the Eocene, land mammal assemblages will know go through a series of gradual changes that will progressively mark the transition with the subsequent faunal stratum, detailed thereafter.

#### Second stratum: Trans-atlantic migrations and faunal 'modernisation' (late Eocene--Late Miocene) {.unnumbered}

Most specialists agree that major re-organisations occurred within South American mammal assemblages near the Eocene--Oligocene boundary (that will be more thoroughly covered in @sec-chap1), marking the onset of Simpson's second faunal stratum (@fig-SALMA). The distinction between the second and the first strata lies in a three-part faunal 'modernisation' [@flynn1998]: (1) emergence of morphological innovations among "original inhabitants", (2) extinction of basal, 'archaic' lineages and (3) higher-level taxonomic origination within "original inhabitants", alongside the arrival and radiation of hystricognathous rodents (Rodentia: Hystricognathi: Caviomorpha) and anthropoid primates (Primates: Anthropoidea) in South America (@fig-SALMA).

```{r, echo=FALSE}

Boundaries between SALMAs were defined on the basis of the most up-to-date literature [*e*.*g*., @bellinzoni2025; @gelfo2009; @dunn2013; @woodburne2014], but note that many intervals lack absolute temporal calibration. Alongside are depicted several key biotic or abiotic upheaval in the Cenozoic history of South American mammals, as well as Simpson's three faunal strata [@simpson1980]. Silhouettes are from Phylopic (credit: Sarah Werning and Kai R. Caspar)."

include_graphics("./Figures/GTS_plot/Detailed_GTS.png")
```

The most notable morphological innovation that could be mentionned is probably the increase in cheek teeth crown height (*i*.*e*., hypsodonty), occurring independently among several (at least six) groups of native ungulates (particularly notoungulates) from the middle Eocene onwards [@croft2020]. The evolution towards hypsodonty in South America is particularly interesting as hypsodont cheek teeth started to be recorded 20 million years before the first reports of hypsodonty outside South America [@garcía-lópez2019]. As they diversified, freshly-arrived caviomorph rodents (see later in this section) also, for some of them, rapidly acquired hypsodont cheek teeth, again, way before any other place in the world (late Oligocene--Early Miocene), as exemplified by the superfamily Chinchilloidea -- see @sec-chap2. The Eocene emergence of hypsodont cheek teeth and their Oligocene spread across lineages has long puzzled South American mammal palaeontologists [*e*.*g*., @billet2009; @croft2003; @reguero2008; -@reguero2010]. Hypsodont cheek teeth are indeed often considered as an indicator of an abrasive diet, typically, incorporating grasses, and thus, have often been related to landscape opening [@stebbins1981]. However, palaeoenvironmental evidence failed to support any concomitant grassland spreading in the regions where the first hypsodont lineages were recorded [*e*.*g*., @kohn2004; -@kohn2015; @strömberg2013]. Now, a consensus emerged in the community, as several lines of evidence instead suggested that the increase in cheek teeth crown height may have instead resulted from grit or volcanic dust consumption [@damuth2011; @jardine2012; @selkin2015; @gomesrodrigues2017; @armella2026].

Besides, by analysing two early Oligocene metatherian communities from Southern South America (one of Tinguirican age, the other being the La Cantera fauna, see @fig-SALMA), @goin2010 reported an important taxonomic turnover occurring among metatherians in the few million years that followed the Eocene--Oligocene transition (EOT). This geological boundary, that will be further explored in @sec-chap1, has been identified as the most intense Cenozoic climatic disruption, as global temperature cooled down by several degrees in a few hundred thousands of years [@coxall2007; @liu2009; @westerhold2020]. The EOT was related to a major faunal turnover among mammalian communities from the Northern hemisphere [@meng1998; @stehlin1909; @stucky2014; @weppe2023]. As an echo to the french expression 'Grande Coupure' [@stehlin1909] used to characterise the mammalian turnover that occurred among European mammal assemblages, @goin2010 thus derived the expression 'Bisagra Patagónica' (*Patagonian hinge*) to qualify the faunal turnover that they characterised.

Next, as we briefly evoked, Simpson's second stratum is also characterised by the abrupt apparition of hystricognathous rodents and anthropoid primates in the South American fossil record [@antoine2012; @bond2015; @seiffert2020; @marivaux2023]. Explaining such an emergence has been one of the most important challenges for South American mammal palaeontology, given that, contrary to xenarthrans (see section of stratum 1), it made no doubt that these groups were the result of a much more recent faunal supply [@simpson1950]. After several decades of intense debate, combined morphological [@hoffstetter1972] and molecular [*e*.*g*., @poux2006] evidence provided strong support for the "rafting hypothesis", in which both groups would have radiated from Afro-Asian ancestors that would have crossed the Atlantic in the Palaeogene [*e*.*g*., @antoine2012; @marivaux2023] (@fig-SALMA).

```{r, echo=FALSE}

Fading colours mean that the group has no known fossil record for the period, but should already exist. Photos were taken from iNaturalist (credit: Jorge Brito, Eduardo Silva Rodriguez, Thiago Chagas). *Wamradolops telloi* cranium comes from @stutz2026, reproduced with permission. The picture of the *Thylacosmilus atrox* cranium was taken by Claire Houck. (**B**) Xenarthra. include_graphics("./Figures/SAM_simplified_chronogram/Composite_figure.png")

```

Despite its wide acceptance, the timing of this fascinating trans-Atlantic journey remains under debate. @seiffert2020 proposed that the global sea-water drop that followed the peri-EOT climate cooling, by reducing the distance between Africa and South America, could have made such a trans-oceanic dispersal easier (assuming the latter to be inversely proportional to the distance between the source and the receiving areas). Such a hypothesis finds support in that, according to a study conducted by the same authors, the oldest fossil evidence for rodents and primates in South America cannot be older than the early Oligocene [@campbell2021]. Conversely, @marivaux2023 proposed that this trans-Atlantic dispersal may have instead occurred 5 million years earlier, near the Middle Eocene Climate Optimum (MECO) [@bohaty2009]. This interval may have been accompanied by intense meteorological episodes in the tropics [@mulch2015], increasing the likelihood of riverbank break-ups, and thus, the formation of floating islands serving as a means for the large-scale dispersal of small-sized mammals, such as rodents or primates [@houle1998]. This hypothesis more adequately explains the high taxonomic diversity displayed by several known early Oligocene rodent communities, accounting for taxa clearly identified as crown caviomorphs, with recognised members of Chinchilloidea [*e*.*g*., @antoine2021; @bertrand2012; @boivin2018; -@boivin2019; @arnal2022 *though some assemblages listed here may be of latest Eocene age*]. Such a diversity would be hard to achieve in the few hundred thousand years separating these assemblages from the EOT. Note that, given the paucity of the primate fossil record in the Palaeogene of South America -- only four specimens assigned to three distantly-related lineages that notably, and contrary to rodents, are not recognised as stem representatives of the extant South American primate radiation, namely, Platyrrhini [@marivaux2023] -- it is currently impossible to apply such a limitation to the primate scenario proposed by @seiffert2020.

In addition, the early Oligocene interval has been recognised as the most likely time frame for the colonisation of the West Indies by several taxa, including crown caviomorph rodents [@marivaux_early_2020], sloths [@tejada2024] as well as other terrestrial taxa [@blackburn2020; @chamberland2018]. These colonisations would have been favoured by the emergence of an ephemeral land bridge between the Greater Antilles and the South American landmass -- the Aves Ridge --, following the aforementioned sea-level drop after the EOT, a hypothesis called GAARlandia [@iturralde-vinent1999; @philippon2020; @cornée2021]. However, it should be mentioned that such a hypothesis has raised criticism [*e*.*g*., @ali2012; @ali2019].

Simpson's second stratum persisted through the Oligocene and the Miocene. Keystone late Oligocene localities, such as Salla (Bolivia) or the Deseado massif (Argentina) (@fig-MapLoc) provided unprecedented insight into South American mammal diversity at that time. In particular, they helped identify the first records of sloths [@pujos2007] as well as to better constraint the diversification of Notoungulata, Litopterna, Astrapoheria and the extinction of Pyrotheria near the Oligocene--Miocene [@croft2020] (@fig-persistence C). Then, from the early Miocene, sampling gets increasingly less temporally discontinuous (@fig-SALMA), thus better constraining our knowledge of the evolution of mammals on the continent. In addition, molecular and fossil data agree that most of the crown extant South American mammal families that survived until the present diverged in the Miocene [@álvarez-carretero2022]. Thus, mammal diversity from the Late Oligocene to the Late Miocene was flourishing, and many invaluable sites or geological formations (*e*.*g*., Santa Cruz Formation, La Venta, Quebrada Honda,... see @fig-MapLoc as well as @croft_horned_2016) yielded precious discoveries attesting that statement.

#### Third stratum: Inter-american exchange, massive faunal disruptions, and establishment of the extant mammal biodiversity (latest Miocene--Present) {.unnumbered}

*Please note that, all-over this manuscript, "North America" will actually refer to North and Central America, roughly, everything above the Isthmus of Panama.*

The flourishing diversity that characterised Simpson's second stratum was massively disrupted in the late Neogene. As seen in @sec-CnzSA, *ca*. 3 Ma, a sustainable landbridge connecting the Americas emerged, known as the Ithmus of Panama. Though noticeable examples of earlier colonisations have been documented in the fossil record [@woodburne2010], it is consensual to consider that the closure of the isthmus of Panama catalysed the admixture between North and South America's endemic mammalian faunas, an event famously known as the 'Great American Biotic Interchange' (GABI) [@webb1985] (@fig-SALMA).

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-GABI
#| out-width: 15cm
#| fig-pos: 'H'
#| fig-cap: "(**A**) Hand-drawing of the North American taxa recorded in the fossil record of South America, hence considered 'newcomers', made by @simpson1950. (**B**) Schematic interpretation of land mammalian exchange across the Americas following the GABI, from [@vrba1992]. All the taxa shown in North America are of South American origin, and vice-versa. *In North America*: 1. glyptodon, 2. anteater, 3. and 7. ground sloths, 4. New-world porcupine, 5. capybara, 6. opossum, 8. armadillo, 9. toxodontid notoungulate. *In South America*: 11. shrew, 12. sigmodontine cricetid, 13. camelid, 14. canid, 15. mustelid, 16. tapir, 17. rabbit, 18. squirrel, 19. peccary, 20. racoon, 21. bear, 22. gomphotheriid, 23. horse, 24. cervid."

include_graphics("./Figures/GABI/GABI_Vrba_Simpson.png")

```

As described by @woodburne2010, although the early phases of the GABI were characterised by roughly symmetrical exchanges (as illustrated by the various groups on @fig-GABI B), during the Pleistocene, the fossil record suggests that an asymmetry of exchange gradually established, with North American taxa colonising South America with a higher success than the other way around. At present, it is estimated that around 50% of South American mammal's generic diversity descend from a North American lineage, whereas this proportion falls down to some 10% when considering genera with a South American ascent living in North America [@webb1991]. The latter proportion is considerably reduced to a few single species when excluding tropical North America, a region that even Wallace recognised as "the portion of the North American continent which belongs zoologically to South America" [@wallace1876]. Consequently, it stands out that the GABI has been highly asymmetric.

What shaped the striking asymmetry of this lineage exchange has been one of the most puzzling issues in South American mammal palaeontology. Several hypotheses have indeed been proposed to explain such an exchange imbalance, that will be intensively reviewed and discussed in @sec-chap3. The first hypotheses formulated involved some kind of competitive superiority of North American taxa compared to South Americans [*e*.*g*., @simpson1950]. Later hypotheses instead placed the emphasis on the role of palaeoclimate change [*e*.*g*., @vrba1992; @webb1991]. @simpson1980 even termed such an exchange a 'fortuitous experiment', arguing that if things were to be repeated, the resulting pattern would thus not necessarily be equivalent. On top of this, confounding effects may arise from megafaunal extinctions [@svenning2024; @hadler2026], several studies arguing that hunting may also have caused the demise of endemic (large-sized) south American clades in South America [@boscaini2025; @prates2021]. Consequently, despite being the subject of a wide range of studies, the drivers behind the asymmetry of the GABI remain non-consensual, and one of the core aims of the present doctoral work is to contribute to a better understanding of this fascinating enigma.

### Challenges for South American mammal palaeontology {#sec-PalChal}

Despite being unique and invaluable, several challenges arise as we intend to work with the South American mammal fossil record, in addition to those previously mentioned arising while using fossils (@sec-FossilBias).

As it shows on the maps displayed on @fig-MapLoc, the fossil record of South American mammals is strikingly uneven across space, with the persistence of a huge gap merely overlapping with the plain of the Amazon river, the Brazilian Highlands and the Guianian Shield (@fig-physiography). Almost 30 years ago, @flynn1998 already pointed the need to fill the pronounced gap in the tropical fossil record of South American mammals, being highly sparse, with the notable exception of the exceptional Miocene fauna from the La Venta locality, Colombia [@carrillo2023] (@fig-MapLoc). This is primarily the result from three factors. First, except along the Andes where the subduction has actively promoted sediment accumulation in the Andean foreland basin (@fig-physiography), tropical South American soils experience little subsidence, and consequently, being less dense than continental crust, hardly can sediments get buried in the Amazonian plain (and thus offering the possibility for fossils to form). Second, tropical soils are markedly more active in terms of microfauna. Decomposition there is thus more efficient than outside the tropics, reducing the probability for a dead body to fossilise. Last, obvious accessibility issues hamper fossil-hunting in the tropical rainforest. Without invoking geopolitical factors, low-latitude fossil-bearing localities from Western Amazonia are indeed almost all located nearby brand-new roads across the forest or along rivers, posing additional logistic issues (@fig-TMB).

Substantial improvements should however be stressed, notably in the Peruvian Amazonia, where exceptional fossil deposits have been found [*reviewed in* @antoine2017]. These are greatly exemplified by the regions of Contamana and Shapaja, where nearly 100 different vertebrate-bearing localities spanning distinct intervals of the Cenozoic have been characterised [@antoine2016; @antoine2021], including CTA-27, where the oldest caviomorph rodent community of the continent was unearthed [@antoine2012]. Significant contributions should also be mentioned from the early Oligocene locality of Santa Rosa [@campbell2004], which yielded two out of the three basalmost primates found in South America to date [@bond2015; @seiffert2020]. Despite all these costly efforts, critical time intervals (such as the middle-late Oligocene or the early Miocene) remain unsampled under tropical latitudes, superimposing on the existing SALMA scale's gaps (depicted in black on @fig-SALMA). Consequently, every palaeontologist who ever worked in tropical South America knows this 'South American mammal fossil record paradox', in which the region encompassing the greatest diversity at the scale of the continent (and even the world, see @fig-maps) is also, by far, the most fossil-poor.

Such an incompleteness was shown to significantly affect upstream macroevolutionary analyses relying on the South American mammal fossil record [@ugarte2025], and should thus be kept in mind when studying the diversification processes in South America based on the fossil record, and thus, throughout the rest of this dissertation.

## Objectives of this doctoral work

This thesis aims to improve the understanding of key periods in South American mammal evolutionary history through an interdisciplinary approach of macroevolution, macroecology and palaeobiology. As detailed over @sec-SAFauna, South American mammal faunas across the Cenozoic are usually summarised by three temporally-successive faunal strata, defined on the basis of shared evolutionary lineages (@fig-SALMA).

The Palaeogene of South America witnessed the transition between Simpson's first stratum, characterised the diversification of the 'Old Timers' (@fig-persistence), and second stratum, in which 'Aliens' (*i*.*e*., anthropoid primates and hystricognathous rodents) diversified meanwhile native lineages experienced a marked faunal 'modernisation' [@croft2008]. Palaeontological evidence [*e*.*g*., @goin2010] suggested that this stratum shift would have occured close to the Eocene--Oligocene Transition (EOT, *ca*. 33.9 Ma), the most dramatic Cenozoic climatic crisis [@coxall2007], associated with a significant turnover -- sometimes even referred to as a mass extinction event -- in the Northern Hemisphere [*e*.*g*., @meng1998; @woodburne2014; @weppe2023]. The absence of integrative continent-scale study leaves many unanswered questions regarding how the EOT affected South American mammalian assemblages. To bring answers to these foundational issues, the @sec-chap1 of this thesis will infer the diversification dynamics of South American mammals over the Eocene--Oligocene interval (*ca*. 56--23 Ma), relying on an unprecedented dataset and cutting-edge preservation-aware methods. In particular, we will ask:

- *Did South American mammals experience a mass extinction at the EOT, as it has been proposed for elsewhere in the world [e.g., @weppe2023]?*
- *Were the changes in the architecture of South American mammal assemblages that followed this inter-strata transition taxonomically, ecologically or latitudinally (i.e., tropical vs. extratropical) homogeneous?*
- *Did the peri-EOT climate cooling affect the dynamics of South American mammal diversification? Can we retrieve a signal of other environmental variables in the Palaeogene dynamics of South American mammal diversification?*

Attention will be further dedicated to post-Palaeogene times (*i*.*e*., < 23 Ma). As introduced in @sec-CnzSA, major environmental upheavals occurred during the Neogene of South America (@fig-SALMA). In particular, along with a long-term global cooling trend [@westerhold2020], the Andean orogeny intensified [@boschman2021], creating a great variety of new climates and, together with sea-level changes, exerting a control on continent-scale hydrographic remodelling (notably, on the emergence and demise of the Pebas MegaWetland System and other marine introgressions, such as the Paranense sea) [@hernández2005]. Whether this unique palaeonvironmental context left an imprint in the macroevolutionary dynamics of South American clades during the Neogene has been often suggested [*e*.*g*., @hoorn2010]. As it happens, this time frame coincides with the spectacular evolution towards gigantism among caviomorph rodents, particularly well exemplified in the superfamily Chinchilloidea, that used to account for some of the largest rodents ever recorded -- up to six times as heavy as the heaviest living rodent, the capybara [@vucetich2015]. In addition, chinchilloid species diversity was much larger in the past than at the present, as attested by their rich fossil record, suggesting this clade experienced an evolutionary decline, thus adding another layer of uncertainty in our understanding of their puzzling macroevolutionary history. Using an unprecedented temporal occurrence database, extensive trait reconstructions and cutting-edge environment- and trait-dependent diversification frameworks, the @sec-chap2 of this thesis will therefore ask:

- *Was the evolution towards large sizes associated with differential diversification rates among Chinchilloidea?*
- *Was chinchilloid decline caused by increased extinction rate, decreased speciation rate, or both?*
- *Was chinchilloid decline selective against particular traits (in particular, body size)?*
- *Did late Cenozoic South American palaeoenvironmental evolution affect the interplay between species diversity and morphological disparity in the Chinchilloidea? If yes, how?*

In a final chapter, attention will be dedicated to one of the most impacting events in the emergence of modern South American mammalian assemblages: the Great American Biotic Interchange [GABI, @webb1985]. This event, characterising the admixture between North and South American faunas that followed the closure of the Isthmus of Panama (@sec-SAFauna) has long puzzled biogeographers, as it resulted in a strikingly imbalanced colonisation success in favour of Northern lineages establishing to the South than the other way around [@webb1976; @marshall1982]. The mechanisms behind such an asymmetry remain poorly resolved, and two contrasting hypotheses have been proposed to this end. Meanwhile the contribution of biotic interactions (mainly, competition, but also predation) has imposed as most direct first-order explanation behind the asymmetry of the GABI, with Nothern lineages outcompeting Southern ones [*e*.*g*., @simpson1950], other authors instead emphasised a contribution of palaeoclimate dynamics [*e*.*g*., @bacon2016; @freitas-oliveira_temperature_2024; @webb1991; @vrba1992]. By means of mechanistic eco-evolutionary simulations ran in a spatially-exlicit landscape made up with high-resolution annual temperature and precipitation layers covering the last five million years, the @sec-chap3 of this thesis will causally assess whether the asymmetry of the GABI can emerge from the exclusive contribution of climatic factors.

The findings produced over this thesis will ultimately be replaced in a broader framework, discussing several perspectives to enhance further macro-eco-evolutionary reflexion on the history of South American mammals along with some methodological considerations.
